answer: The saddler counts the stitches in every bridle he makes and enters the count in his stitch book against the horse it serves. A glacier bridle bought from another saddler fails the book: at the cedar of the stitches the work must match the saddler's own hand, and a bought bridle stitches unevenly. Forging a bridle means hiring a saddler, cutting false leather and paying 9,900 in hide and wages, and the tide entry in the stitch book is kept for ten years, so a bridle whose stitches were never counted is cut apart.
